prompt:
Which of these formulas are **tautologies** (true in every row)? Select all that apply.

*Symbols: ¬ means NOT; ∧ means AND; ∨ means OR (inclusive); → means "implies" (if ... then).*

options.explanation: Correct. If q is true, p implies q is true. If q is false, q implies p is true. Either way one disjunct holds.
Not a tautology. It assumes an implication gives you its converse. In the row p false, q true, p implies q is true but q implies p is false, so the whole formula is false.

options.text: ((p implies q) and p) implies q
options.explanation: Correct. This is modus ponens written as a formula: whenever both premises are true, q is true.

options.text: ((p implies q) and q) implies p
options.explanation: Not a tautology. This is affirming the consequent. Row p equals F, q equals T makes both premises true and the conclusion false.
Correct. The premise p and not p is false in every row, so the implication is vacuously true everywhere. From a contradiction, anything follows.

workedExample:
The symbols used in the options:

```formula
p → q
(p → q) ∧ p
p ∧ ¬p
where
p, q: propositions, each true (T) or false (F)
→: implies: false only when the left side is true and the right side false
∧: AND: true only when both sides are true
∨: OR: true when at least one side is true
¬: NOT: ¬p is true exactly when p is false
T: true
F: false
In words: an implication can only fail with a true left side and a false right side, so to break a formula of the form "X → Y" you need a row where X is true and Y is false.
```

Check each option with the row most likely to break it:

| Option | Looking for a breaking row | Found? |
|---|---|---|
| A | Needs both disjuncts false. p implies q is false only for p true, q false, and then q implies p is true | None |
| B | p false, q true: left side true, right side false | Yes |
| C | Needs q false with both premises true, but p true and q false makes p implies q false | None |
| D | p false, q true: both premises true, conclusion false | Yes |
| E | The premise p and not p is never true | None |

A, C and E have no breaking row, so they are tautologies.
